**An Alabama firefighter saw children missing medical care because they had no ride. So he started driving them himself**

By [Staff Writer]

BIRMINGHAM, Alabama — For many families, a doctor’s appointment is a matter of scheduling, insurance and time off work. But for some children in Alabama, the biggest barrier has been much simpler: getting there.

Russell Jackson, an Alabama firefighter, saw that problem up close — children who needed routine checkups, specialist visits, therapy or other medical care, but whose families had no reliable transportation to reach appointments. In response, he founded **Kid One Transport**, an organization dedicated to helping children get to medical care when transportation stands in the way.

The idea was rooted in a basic belief: a child’s health should not depend on whether a parent owns a car, has gas money or can find someone to drive them across town — or across the state.

Kid One Transport was created to bridge that gap. The organization provides transportation for children and expectant mothers who need help getting to medical appointments, serving families who might otherwise be forced to postpone or miss care altogether.

For low-income families, transportation can be one of the most overlooked obstacles in health care. A missed appointment can mean delayed diagnoses, interrupted treatments or worsening health conditions. For children with chronic illnesses or specialized needs, the consequences can be especially serious.

Jackson’s work as a firefighter placed him in a profession built around emergency response. But Kid One Transport reflects a different kind of rescue — one that happens before a crisis, by making sure children can access preventive and ongoing medical care.

What began as one man’s effort to solve a visible community problem grew into a service focused on removing a barrier many families face in silence. The mission is straightforward but powerful: no child should miss essential health care because there is no way to get there.

In Alabama, where rural distances and poverty can complicate access to medical services, transportation assistance can make the difference between an appointment kept and an appointment lost. Kid One Transport’s role is not only logistical; for families under stress, it can also offer reassurance that they are not alone.

Jackson’s story is a reminder that some of the most meaningful public health solutions begin with someone noticing what others overlook.

A firefighter is trained to respond when help is needed. Through Kid One Transport, Russell Jackson found another way to answer the call — one ride, one child and one appointment at a time.

**In Birmingham, a Ride Becomes a Lifeline: How Kid One Transport Connects Alabama Children to Health Care**

BIRMINGHAM, Ala. — On many mornings in Alabama, a child’s medical appointment does not begin in a waiting room. It begins before sunrise, down a gravel road, at the end of a driveway where a parent is watching for a van.

For families across rural Alabama, getting to a doctor can be the hardest part of getting well. Pediatric specialists are often concentrated in Birmingham, Montgomery, Huntsville, Mobile or other regional hubs, while many children who need care live an hour or more away. Public transportation is limited or nonexistent in much of the state. A parent may not own a reliable car, may be unable to take time off work, or may have to choose between paying for gas and paying for groceries.

That gap — between a medical need and a way to reach it — is the problem Kid One Transport was created to solve.

Based in Birmingham, Kid One Transport is a nonprofit organization that provides transportation for children and expectant mothers who need access to health care. Its vans carry patients to appointments for primary care, specialty treatment, dental visits, counseling, therapy, prenatal care and follow-up services. For many families, the ride is not a convenience. It is the difference between receiving care and going without it.

The organization traces its origins to Russell Jackson, who founded Kid One Transport after recognizing that many Alabama children were missing medical appointments not because their families were indifferent, but because they had no dependable way to get there. Jackson saw transportation as a hidden barrier in the health-care system — one that rarely appeared on a diagnosis, but could determine whether a child’s asthma was managed, whether a dental infection was treated, whether a newborn received follow-up care, or whether a pregnant mother made it to a prenatal visit.

His idea was straightforward: if transportation was keeping children from doctors, then the transportation itself had to become part of the health-care response.

In a state where rural poverty, long distances and limited transit overlap, that mission quickly became urgent.

Alabama’s rural transportation problem is not simply about geography. It is about infrastructure, economics and health equity. Many small communities have no bus routes, no train service and few affordable ride options. Some families depend on relatives, neighbors or church members for transportation. Others rely on aging vehicles that may not survive a long trip to Birmingham. A missed appointment can trigger a chain reaction: delayed diagnosis, worsening symptoms, emergency-room visits, missed school days and higher medical costs.

For children with chronic illnesses, the stakes are especially high. A child with diabetes may need regular monitoring. A child with cancer may need repeated treatments. A child recovering from surgery may need follow-up care. A child with developmental delays may need therapy appointments that cannot be skipped without consequences. In each case, consistency matters — and consistency is difficult when transportation is uncertain.

Kid One Transport steps into that uncertainty.

The organization works with families, medical providers and social service agencies to coordinate rides. Its drivers often travel long distances, picking up children and caregivers in rural counties and bringing them to clinics and hospitals in Birmingham and elsewhere. The work can involve early mornings, long days and complex scheduling, particularly when multiple children from different communities need to reach appointments at different times.

But the impact is measured in more than miles.

For a parent, a Kid One ride can mean not having to reschedule a specialist visit that took months to secure. For a physician, it can mean seeing a patient before a condition becomes an emergency. For a child, it can mean relief from pain, better management of a chronic condition, or simply the chance to grow up healthier.

Transportation is one of the less visible social determinants of health, but its effects are immediate. A child cannot benefit from a prescription that is never written, a therapy session never attended, or a diagnosis never made. In rural communities, the distance to care can function like a wall. Kid One’s mission is to lower that wall, one trip at a time.

The need is particularly pronounced in Alabama’s Black Belt and other rural regions where poverty rates are high and medical resources are scarce. Hospitals have closed or reduced services in many rural areas across the South, leaving families to travel farther for pediatric care. Even when local clinics exist, specialized care — cardiology, neurology, oncology, orthopedics, behavioral health — is often available only in larger cities.

Birmingham, with institutions such as Children’s of Alabama and UAB-related medical services, serves as a major health-care destination for families across the state. But for a family without a working car, Birmingham might as well be hundreds of miles farther away.

That is the reality Kid One Transport was built around.

The organization’s work also reflects a broader understanding of children’s health: medical care does not begin and end inside a clinic. It depends on whether families can access appointments, understand treatment plans, return for follow-up care and maintain contact with providers. Transportation is a practical service, but it also offers stability to families navigating illness, poverty and distance at the same time.

For expectant mothers, transportation can be just as critical. Regular prenatal care is associated with better outcomes for mothers and infants, yet rural women often face significant obstacles getting to appointments. A ride to prenatal care can help identify complications earlier, support healthier pregnancies and reduce risks for newborns.

For children, early and consistent care can prevent small problems from becoming lifelong ones.

That is why Kid One’s model has drawn support from donors, health-care partners and community organizations. It occupies a space that is both simple and essential: connecting families to the care that already exists but remains out of reach without a ride.

In an era when health-care debates often focus on insurance, hospitals and costs, Kid One Transport highlights a quieter truth. Coverage matters, but so does access. A Medicaid card, a referral or an appointment reminder cannot drive a child from a rural county to Birmingham. Without transportation, the promise of care may remain theoretical.

Russell Jackson’s founding insight was that a missed appointment is not always a personal failure. Sometimes it is a systems failure. Kid One Transport was created to repair that failure in the most direct way possible — by showing up at the door.

Today, the sight of a Kid One van on Alabama roads represents more than a ride. It represents a bridge between rural communities and urban medical centers, between poverty and treatment, between a child’s diagnosis and a child’s chance to heal.

For families who have exhausted every other option, that bridge can be life-changing.

And in Birmingham, where so much of Alabama’s pediatric specialty care is concentrated, the mission remains clear: no child’s health should depend on whether their family has a car, a full gas tank or a way out of town.

## After one heartbreaking call, he left firefighting. Now he drives Alabama children toward hope.

For years, the sound of a firehouse alarm meant one thing to Marcus Hill: someone needed help, and he was going.

As a firefighter in central Alabama, Hill had pulled people from wrecked cars, battled house fires in the punishing summer heat, and stood with families on the worst days of their lives. He thought he had learned how to carry the weight.

Then came the call he couldn’t leave behind.

It was a late-night emergency involving a child — the kind first responders train for but never forget. Hill did his job. He followed protocol. He stayed calm because everyone around him needed him to be calm.

But in the days that followed, the images replayed in his mind. Sleep became difficult. The firehouse, once a place of purpose and brotherhood, began to feel like a reminder of grief.

“I could handle danger,” Hill said. “What I couldn’t handle was feeling like I got there too late.”

Eventually, Hill made the painful decision to leave firefighting. He stepped away from the career he loved, unsure of what would come next. But even as he tried to heal, one thought kept returning: What if he could still help children — not at the moment of crisis, but before life became one?

That question became the beginning of Miles for Smiles Alabama, a nonprofit van service that provides free transportation for children and families in need.

Today, Hill spends his days behind the wheel of a donated passenger van, driving children to medical appointments, counseling sessions, after-school programs, food pantries, tutoring, and safe visits with relatives. Many of the families he serves live in rural communities where public transportation is limited or nonexistent. For them, a missed ride can mean a missed diagnosis, a missed meal, or a missed opportunity.

“A lot of people don’t realize how much depends on transportation,” Hill said. “If a child can’t get to the doctor, if a mother can’t get her son to therapy, if a grandmother can’t get her grandkids to school activities — that can change everything.”

Hill founded the nonprofit with little more than a used van, a notebook full of names, and a conviction that no child should suffer because their family lacked a reliable way to get somewhere. At first, he handled every ride himself. He answered calls at all hours, mapped routes across several counties, and often paid for gas out of his own pocket.

Word spread quickly.

A school counselor called about a student who needed weekly trauma counseling but had no ride. A clinic asked if Hill could bring a child in for follow-up treatment. A church connected him with a family whose car had broken down months earlier. Each request, Hill said, reminded him why he had started.

One of those children was 9-year-old Jayden, whose asthma required regular appointments more than 30 miles from home. His mother, working part-time and caring for three children, had already missed multiple visits because she couldn’t find transportation.

Hill began driving Jayden and his mother to the clinic twice a month.

“He didn’t just give us a ride,” Jayden’s mother said. “He gave me peace of mind. He made my son feel like he mattered.”

The van has become more than transportation. Hill keeps snacks, bottled water, blankets, books, and small toys inside. Children know he’ll greet them by name. Parents know he’ll wait through long appointments without complaint. On some rides, the van is quiet. On others, children talk freely about school, fears, dreams, and the things they don’t always have space to say elsewhere.

Hill says listening is part of the work.

“When I was a firefighter, I showed up when everything was falling apart,” he said. “Now I get to show up earlier. I get to be part of keeping things from falling apart.”

The need continues to grow. Hill’s nonprofit now coordinates with schools, churches, clinics, and social workers across the region. Volunteers help schedule rides, maintain the van, and raise money for fuel, insurance, and repairs. Hill hopes to add more vehicles so the organization can serve additional counties throughout Alabama.

Still, he says the mission will remain personal.

He carries the memory of that final traumatic call with him — not as something he has escaped, but as something that reshaped his understanding of service. Firefighting taught him courage. Loss taught him urgency. The children he drives now have taught him that healing can come mile by mile.

“I thought leaving the fire department meant I was done helping people,” Hill said. “But I wasn’t done. I just had to find a different way to answer the call.”

And on Alabama back roads, in a van filled with children’s laughter, appointment reminders, and second chances, Marcus Hill is still answering.

**Russell Jackson’s Mission to Make Sure Alabama Children Don’t Miss Care for Lack of a Ride**

For Russell Jackson, the problem was never simply transportation. It was access — to doctors, to treatment, to a chance at a healthier life.

Jackson is the driving force behind **Kid One Transport**, an Alabama nonprofit built around a stark reality: tens of thousands of children in the state need medical care but cannot reliably get to it. An estimated **80,000 Alabama children live in households without cars**, a barrier that can turn a routine checkup, specialist visit, therapy appointment or follow-up exam into an impossible trip.

Kid One Transport was created to close that gap. The organization provides rides for children and expectant mothers who otherwise might miss critical medical appointments because their families lack dependable transportation. Since its founding, Kid One has provided more than **16,000 rides**, helping families reach hospitals, clinics, dentists, therapists and other health-care providers across Alabama.

Jackson’s commitment to the work was shaped by a personal turning point: the death of a **2-year-old child** whose life might have been different had access to timely medical care not been so difficult. The loss crystallized for him how something as ordinary as a ride could become a matter of life and death.

That realization became the moral center of Kid One Transport. Jackson saw that medical advice alone was not enough if a family had no way to act on it. A doctor’s appointment on the calendar meant little without a car in the driveway, gas money in a pocket or public transit that reached the clinic.

The nonprofit’s model is straightforward but powerful: remove transportation as a reason children go untreated. For families facing poverty, rural isolation or other barriers, Kid One offers more than a trip from one address to another. It offers continuity of care, relief from missed appointments and, in many cases, peace of mind.

Jackson’s work highlights a quieter side of health care — the logistics that determine whether patients ever reach the exam room. In a state where many communities are spread out and services can be far from home, transportation is not a convenience. It is part of the care itself.

Through Kid One Transport, Jackson has turned grief into service and a transportation problem into a public-health mission. Each ride represents a child who did not have to miss care simply because no one could get them there.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a CNN news story about how lack of transportation prevents rural Alabama children from getting medical care and how former firefighter Russell Jackson addressed the issue through Kid One Transport.
counterfactuals.output:
**Rural Alabama children are missing doctor’s appointments because they don’t have a ride. One former firefighter built a solution.**

*By [Your Name], CNN-style news feature*

In many parts of rural Alabama, the distance between a sick child and a doctor’s office can be measured not just in miles — but in access.

For families without reliable cars, money for gas or nearby public transportation, a routine medical appointment can become nearly impossible. A child may need a follow-up visit after surgery, dental care, therapy, cancer treatment or a specialist hours away. But in communities where buses don’t run and clinics are far apart, getting care often depends on one simple question: *Who can drive?*

That gap is what former firefighter Russell Jackson set out to address through **Kid One Transport**, an Alabama nonprofit that provides transportation for children and expectant mothers who need medical care but have no dependable way to get there.

The organization helps families travel to appointments for doctor visits, dental treatment, mental health services, physical therapy and other essential care. For many parents, especially in rural counties, the service can mean the difference between a child receiving timely treatment or going without it.

Transportation barriers are a persistent challenge across rural Alabama. Families may live far from pediatric specialists, and public transit options are limited or nonexistent. Some parents work hourly jobs and cannot afford to miss shifts. Others may have a vehicle that is unreliable, no money for fuel, or no support network available to help with long medical trips.

The consequences can be serious. Missed appointments can delay diagnoses, worsen chronic conditions and force families to rely on emergency rooms instead of preventive care. For children with ongoing medical needs, repeated missed visits can set back treatment and recovery.

Jackson’s background as a firefighter gave him firsthand experience with emergencies — and with the reality that many health crises are made worse when people cannot access care early. Kid One Transport was created to intervene before a medical problem becomes an emergency.

The nonprofit coordinates rides so children and pregnant women can reach hospitals, clinics and specialty providers across Alabama. Its work is especially important in rural areas, where a “nearby” appointment may still require hours on the road.

For families served by Kid One Transport, the impact is practical and immediate: a child gets to chemotherapy, a mother-to-be gets prenatal care, a teenager gets counseling, or a patient makes it to a specialist appointment that would otherwise be missed.

Health advocates say transportation is one of the most overlooked barriers in medicine. A doctor can prescribe treatment, but that treatment only matters if the patient can physically get to the office, hospital or clinic.

Kid One Transport’s mission is built around that reality. By focusing on transportation, the organization addresses a basic but often hidden part of health care access — the ride itself.

In rural Alabama, where poverty, distance and limited transit can combine to keep children from medical care, Jackson’s solution is straightforward: make sure the child gets there.

And for families who have run out of options, that ride can be life-changing.
